1.pericope_label: The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord: to do justice and judgment is more acceptable than sacrifice

schools.summary: Henry uses the irrigation figure to protect the freedom of the will, since directing water alters neither its nature nor its liberty, infers from the preference of justice to sacrifice that the excellence of the ceremonial was not innate nor its obligation perpetual, uses both the ploughing and the lamp in one note on the fourth verse, and compresses the fifth into the maxim that forecast is as good as work.

Gill abandons the irrigation figure of the first verse and takes the water for instability, the heart of a king being fluid and fluctuating though God can settle it, and finds every man conceited of his own way and not easily persuaded off it.

Clarke describes the canals and sluices of eastern irrigation and applies the figure to royal bounty bestowed on a favourite, takes the disputed word of the fourth verse as the lamp and reads it of the prosperity and posterity of the wicked, and reports manuscripts, editions and versions reading the snares of death in the sixth verse rather than those who seek it; Wesley makes the ploughing the ordinary lawful actions of ungodly men, sinful because managed without regard to God’s glory.

Ellicott reads the first verse of a heart turned toward one suppliant and then another, renders the fourth verse as the work of the wicked while allowing lamp as a possible sense, and gathers three proverbial sayings about haste from as many languages; Keil and Delitzsch place the third verse in the wisdom tradition of preferring moral obedience to cultic works, canvass every sense of the disputed word in the fourth and reach none, gather the same cluster of sayings about haste, and report the text of the sixth verse unsettled.

debates: What is the ploughing of the wicked? Ellicott makes it their work, all they do, while allowing that the word may signify a lamp; Clarke takes the lamp and reads it of the prosperity and posterity of the wicked; Wesley makes it their civil and natural actions, lawful in themselves but sinful as managed without regard to God’s glory; Henry uses both senses in one note, having them always ploughing and plotting and then declaring that the light of the wicked is sin; Keil and Delitzsch canvass the options at length, reject brilliant prosperity and a flaming spirit as contrary to the usual metaphor, reject the sense of yoke as not Hebrew, and settle nothing.

How is the first verse’s figure to be applied? Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley take it of irrigation canals and apply it to a king’s favour directed now to one suppliant and now to another; Henry takes the same practice but applies it to the will, since directing water puts no force upon its nature; Gill abandons irrigation and reads the water as instability which God can settle and keep within bounds.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott independently gather the same cluster of proverbial sayings about haste from three languages, Keil and Delitzsch adding a modern poet’s lines about revolving like the stars, without haste but without rest.

Clarke reports that several manuscripts, some ancient editions and four versions read the snares of death in the sixth verse rather than those who seek death, so that the gainer pursues vanity into the snares; Keil and Delitzsch report the same divided evidence and say the text is unsettled.
Henry infers from the preference of justice to sacrifice that the excellence of the ceremonial institutions was not innate nor the obligation to them perpetual.
themes: a will directed without being forced
ritual weighed against conduct and found lighter
one consonant read as ploughing, as lamp and as prosperity
haste and delay balanced in three languages
a variant that turns seekers into snares

7.pericope_label: The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them: the soul of the wicked desireth evil

schools.summary: Henry holds that getting money by lying is downright robbery, since cheating is stealing and a man might as well pick a pocket as impose by a lie in a bargain, works the word strange three ways in the eighth verse, gets his sense of the wide house from its meaning a house of society for entertaining friends, and draws from the scorner’s punishment the rule that it is no injustice to take to ourselves a lesson designed for another.

Gill produces a fourth sense of the verb in the seventh verse on a Jewish commentator’s authority, that it means to saw or dissect, so that conscience draws a saw to and fro over such men, and describes the flat roofs of that country as places of retirement enclosed with battlements.

Clarke takes the verb of the seventh verse as terrifying, renders the wide house a house of fellowship or lodging-house occupied by several families and reports an old English manuscript Bible reading it a house of feasting, and sets a limit to the punishment of scorners that no one else here approaches, that only blasphemy against God and the Bible should be so dealt with and that the state should not meddle with private opinion; Wesley reads the way of man as estranged from God.

Ellicott renders the seventh verse of their violence and offers as an alternative to froward and strange that the way is tortuous of a man laden with sin, and lists the uses of the flat housetop for exercise, sleeping, devotion and domestic purposes; Keil and Delitzsch set out three homonymous roots behind the verb of the seventh verse, connect the hapax of the eighth with being charged with a crime, name the joining of wife and house a figure setting two ideas side by side where our language would subordinate one, and find the interchange of tenses in the tenth verse deliberate.

debates: What does the verb of the seventh verse mean? Keil and Delitzsch set out three roots behind it, one giving teareth or draggeth away, which they prefer with an old Latin and a Greek translator; another giving to dwell or sojourn, which the older Greek version followed; and a third giving to dread, which two later versions took, so that the violence terrifies the violent. Clarke follows the third; Gill adds a fourth from a Jewish commentator, that the word means to saw or dissect.

What is the house of the ninth verse? Keil and Delitzsch make it a house held in common; Clarke a house of fellowship or lodging-house occupied by several families, and reports an old English Bible reading it a house of feasting; Henry keeps the wide house and takes the word to mean a house of society in which a man may entertain his friends, which the affliction described renders unsociable.
outliers: Clarke, having granted that one public punishment of a scorner may be a blessing to thousands, sets a limit to it, that only blasphemy against God and the Bible should be so punished and that private opinion the state should not meddle with.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the mocker himself gains nothing by his punishment, being incorrigible, but that the punishment is not lost, since as a warning example it teaches the simple who might otherwise be drawn into the same frivolity.
Henry holds that cheating is stealing, and that a man might as well pick another’s pocket as impose on him by a lie in making a bargain.
themes: one verb resolved into three unrelated roots
crookedness attributed to guilt rather than to strangeness
a shared house preferred to a spacious one
character stated in one tense and consequence in another
public punishment allowed and private opinion protected

13.pericope_label: Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor: a gift in secret pacifieth anger

schools.summary: Henry pictures the man who turns the poor from his door and will not heed what he cannot avoid hearing, describes the manners of a secret gift precisely and notes that covetousness is a master-sin commanding the other lusts, offers both senses of the terror in the fifteenth verse, makes the congregation of the dead the sinners of the old world swept away by the flood, and allows the delights of sense soberly used while locating the fault in setting the heart upon them.

Gill takes the verb of the fourteenth verse as extinguishing on the authority of two versions and finds it fitting since anger is a fire in the breast, notes that others render it bringing the anger down, observes that some understand the verse of a bribe to a judge, and reads the ransom of the eighteenth verse as substitution in trouble, naming several instances.

Clarke refers the first verse to the priest and the Levite and then declares the words quite plain with no difficulty in them, holds that the word for the congregation means the lost and that the passage implies their conscious existence while allowing it may include the fallen angels, quotes an old English manuscript Bible on the same verse, and is severest on the lover of pleasure, holding him so deservedly poor as to have none to pity him; Wesley notes that secrecy makes the gift more acceptable.

Ellicott takes the second half of the fifteenth verse to mean that doing right is itself a terror to the workers of iniquity, who fear ruin if they do not cheat when they can, reads the congregation of the dead as exclusion from the resurrection and calls the verse a prophecy of retribution after death, and reckons the price of a Gospel ointment in his own currency at about a year’s wages of a labourer; Keil and Delitzsch confess that no preposition of their language or ours renders the fullness of one in the thirteenth verse, and set out the range of the verb in the fourteenth from extinguishing to bending down.

debates: What is the terror of the fifteenth verse? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take it that doing right is itself the terror to the workers of iniquity, injustice having become their second nature so that they fear ruin if they do not cheat their neighbours when they can; Henry gives both this and the plainer sense, that it terrifies them to see the laws executed against vice and profaneness.

Who compose the congregation of the dead? Henry makes them the sinners of the old world swept away by the flood, and says the wanderer shall rest there but not in peace; Clarke agrees, holds the word to mean the lost and the passage to imply their conscious existence, and allows that the assembly may also include the fallen angels; Ellicott takes it forward instead, that such a man will have no part in the resurrection, and calls the verse a prophecy of retribution after death.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch stop over a single preposition in the thirteenth verse and confess that no preposition of their language or of ours conveys its fullness, where Clarke on the same verse declares the words quite plain and the passage free of difficulty.

Keil and Delitzsch explain how the verb of the fourteenth verse can mean both to extinguish and to bend down, since the later word means to cover by turning a vessel over, which done to a candle amounts to putting it out.

Henry describes the manners of a secret gift, that the taker would not be thought to covet it, nor known to receive it, nor be willingly beholden to a man he has been offended with, but that if it is done privately all is well.
Ellicott reckons the price of the ointment named in the Gospels in his own currency, making it about a year’s wages of a day labourer.
themes: a text called plain by one reader and untranslatable by another
a gift that quenches anger or bends it down
justice itself made terrible to the unjust
a company of the dead variously peopled
pleasure allowed in use and forbidden as an object

19.pericope_label: It is better to dwell in the wilderness: a wise man scaleth the city of the mighty

schools.summary: Henry holds that those cannot dwell in peace who cannot dwell in love, and that those who are one flesh without being one spirit have no joy of their union, prefers an old-fashioned house well furnished to a fine modern one with sorry housekeeping, converts the taking of a city into a conquest by strength of reason nobler than any got by arms, and gives the two-way rule that keeping the heart keeps the tongue from sin and keeping the tongue keeps the heart from trouble.

Gill observes that the word for wilderness may signify the place where no speech is, so that a voiceless solitude is preferred to a scolding voice, notes that lawful treasure may be desired and laid up while riches of grace are more desirable still, and applies the taking of the city to Christ entering a heart held by the strong man armed.

Clarke keeps the taking of the city to siegecraft and remarks what skill does in the fortification and reduction of strong places; Wesley explains that oil is singled out because it formed a considerable part of the wealth of those countries, and glosses the strength cast down as the strongest defences in which the citizens trusted.

Ellicott reads the three rewards of the twenty-first verse twice over, first as length of days, power to live uprightly and present honour, then as eternal life, forgiveness and honour at the last day; Keil and Delitzsch treat the nineteenth verse as the collector’s new addition and dismiss a witticism about it, dispute the pointing of the twentieth, distinguish the two virtues pursued in the twenty-first, and identify the scorner of the twenty-fourth with the free-thinkers of their own recent centuries.

debates: What is found by him who follows after righteousness, when righteousness is also what he pursues? Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two things pursued, one being conduct proceeding from self-denying love and the other conduct proceeding from sympathy that puts itself in another’s place; Ellicott reads the three rewards twice over, first of length of days and present honour and then of eternal life, forgiveness of sins and honour at the last day; Henry resolves it as grace given to do good and the pleasure of doing it.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar’s witticism that the corner of the roof having been used already, the author of this doublet must look further out for a lonely seat, and dismiss it as piquant but devoid of thought, since it assumes without asking whether both proverbs have the same author and were coined at the same time.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the scorner of the twenty-fourth verse with the free-thinkers of their own recent centuries, who subject the faith of the church to destructive criticism, holding that the ancient name was given to men who mockingly set themselves above revealed religion and prophecy.
Gill observes that the word for wilderness may signify the place where no speech is heard, so that a voiceless solitude is what the proverb prefers.
Henry converts the scaling of a city into a conquest of the affections by strength of reason, which he calls nobler than any conquest got by strength of arms.
themes: a repeated proverb treated as evidence about a collection
solitude preferred for its silence
one virtue both pursued and received
a siege read as an argument
an ancient name for the mocker matched with a modern one

25.pericope_label: The desire of the slothful killeth him: the horse is prepared against the day of battle

schools.summary: Henry has the sluggard starved by his sloth and stabbed by his desires at once, since the hands refuse to labour while the heart keeps coveting, says that many can freely give God their beasts, their lips and their knees who would not give him their hearts, and draws the contrast of the last verses from two questions, the wicked man asking what he has a mind to and the upright what God requires of him.

Gill takes the sluggard’s desire to fret him to death or drive him to unlawful methods, applies the false witness to teachers of false doctrine as well as to perjurers, and reads the horse as standing for all other military preparation and instruments of war.

Clarke names the cases in which a sacrifice is doubly abominable, of goods ill-gotten or offered by constraint of custom, reports upwards of fifty manuscripts and several editions reading that the upright understands his way rather than directs it, and observes that horses were forbidden to that people by divine command and not used before the reign of the king named in the book’s title, who transgressed the command and yet allows here that a horse is a vain thing for safety; Wesley reads the sacrifice as offered to cover or countenance a wicked design.

Ellicott holds the offerer of the twenty-seventh verse to be plotting future wickedness or thinking to make God his confederate by overlooking sin for a gift, and glosses the obscure twenty-eighth verse so that the careful hearer speaks constantly in the sense that his testimony will outlive him; Keil and Delitzsch correct a scholar’s account of the sluggard’s desire, read the preposition of the twenty-seventh verse as one of price so that the sacrifice pays for the crime, dismiss a conjecture on the twenty-eighth, and run a group of proverbs across the chapter boundary.

debates: What is meant by bringing a sacrifice with a wicked mind? Keil and Delitzsch deny that the preposition is one of manner and make it one of price, so that the sacrifice is brought as payment for the crime intended; Ellicott arrives independently at the same place, that the offerer plots future wickedness or thinks by the gift to make God overlook his sin and so become as it were his confederate; Clarke adds offerings of goods ill-gotten or made by constraint of custom, and Wesley one made to cover or countenance a wicked design.

What does the twenty-eighth verse mean by speaking constantly? Keil and Delitzsch reject a conjecture that would make it the man who rejoices to deliver, asking where the verb ever bears that sense, and take the man to be one who hears before he speaks; Ellicott glosses it that he who hears carefully and repeats accurately will have a testimony that lives after him; Wesley takes it that he always affirms the same thing.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch correct a scholar who said that the sluggard’s desire kills him as hunger does, answering that in that case it is not the desire that kills him but the impossibility of satisfying it.

Clarke observes that horses were forbidden that people by divine command and were not used before the reign of the king to whom this book is ascribed, who transgressed the command, and who nonetheless allows here that a horse is a vain thing for safety.
Henry observes that many can freely give God their beasts, their lips and their knees who would not give him their hearts.
Keil and Delitzsch ask where in all the world the verb proposed by one conjecture on the twenty-eighth verse ever means to deliver.
themes: sloth starving a man while desire stabs him
an offering read as the price of a crime
testimony that outlives the witness
a hardened face set against a considered way
a proverb that convicts the king it is ascribed to
